description: Dense continuous solenoid winding with two external leads, four outside suspended needles and the partly obscured internal needle. Preserve positions without inventing source current, coil poles or an external closed circuit.

authoritativeText.text:
A small current-carrying loop that can turn freely experiences an action that tends to orient it in a magnetic field.
A small magnetic needle also takes an orientation in the field; their stable orientations help us determine the field direction.
The quantity describing the magnetic field has a direction as well as a magnitude, so it is represented by the magnetic flux density vector.

A line perpendicular to the plane of a loop is called a normal, but a plane has two opposite normal directions.
Choose the normal $\vec n$ using the right-hand screw rule in Figure 243: turn the handle in the direction of the current around the loop, and the screw advances in the chosen normal direction.
When a small loop is in stable equilibrium in an approximately uniform external magnetic field, this chosen normal points in the direction of the magnetic flux density vector at the loop.
While the loop is still turning, its instantaneous normal must not simply be identified with the external field direction.

A small loop can probe the magnetic field direction if it is free to turn and its oscillations have diminished so that it reaches stable equilibrium.
Then use the current direction and the right-hand screw rule to determine the normal direction.
This method uses the orientation of the loop, not motion that draws the loop toward the field source.

This orientation can also be used to study the weak magnetic field of Earth.
The textbook describes using a coil with more turns or a larger current to make the orienting effect easier to observe; it does not say that every field measurement requires a very large current.
This Earth-field demonstration can also use a comparatively large coil, provided the external field is still approximately uniform over the coil.
The coil in Figure 245 can turn about both vertical and horizontal axes, so it can show the field direction tilted relative to the ground.
The field at the region discussed in the textbook tilts downward toward the ground; different regions do not all have the same direction or amount of tilt.

A magnetic needle is a permanent magnet with an $S$ pole and an $N$ pole.
At the same location in a magnetic field, allow it to turn freely and settle into stable equilibrium: the direction from its $S$ pole toward its $N$ pole agrees with the normal $\vec n$ of the stable small loop in Figure 244.
The direction from $S$ to $N$ on the stable needle can therefore also determine the direction of the magnetic flux density vector.

Figure 246 repeats the orientation experiment with a magnetic needle to probe the direction of the local magnetic field of Earth.
An ordinary needle that turns only in a horizontal plane mainly shows the horizontal direction; a needle that can also turn about a horizontal axis can show the tilt relative to the ground.
Figure 247 illustrates this tilted orientation.

Near a long straight wire carrying current, a magnetic needle settles along a tangent to a circle centered on the wire, as in Figure 248.
The circle lies in a plane perpendicular to the wire; the field direction at each point is tangent to the circle, not toward the wire.
Let a right-handed screw advance in the current direction: the turning direction of its handle gives the direction of the surrounding magnetic field.
This rule uses conventional current direction; the electron-motion direction cannot be substituted without reversing the relevant direction.

Magnetic needles or small current-carrying loops can probe other fields too, such as the field of the current-carrying solenoid in Figure 249.
A solenoid is formed by winding a wire into a series of loops; placing a needle at different locations lets us compare the local field directions.

The similar behavior of a magnetic needle and a small current loop reflects that both can act as magnetic dipoles and orient in an external field.
The textbook uses the picture of many tiny closed currents to explain permanent magnets; this is a model that helps us reason, while modern physics also considers microscopic magnetic moments and their alignment within a material.
The model does not mean that a needle literally contains tiny metal-wire coils; the following chapter discusses the related ideas.
